blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: An association between two variables, however strong or statistically significant, does not by itself establish that one causes the other. Four alternative explanations must be weighed first: chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A strong r, or a significant chi-square test of independence (recall §10.6.1), says that two variables move together. It says nothing about why.

  1. Chance. Test enough pairs of variables and some will correlate by accident (recall §8.3 and the multiplicity point in §8.5). The p-value and confidence interval address this explanation, and only this one.
  2. Bias. A systematic error in how people were selected (selection bias) or how the variables were measured (information bias) can create or hide an association. Bias is taken up in Chapter 17 (§17.2).
  3. Confounding. A third variable causes both (§11.6).
  4. Reverse causation. The outcome causes the “exposure”. A cross-sectional survey that finds lower physical activity among people with arthritis cannot say which came first.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together across the months of the year. Ice cream does not cause drowning: hot weather drives both. In a district, the number of health workers correlates positively with the recorded disease burden. More health workers do not cause disease. Districts with more disease may be sent more staff (reverse causation), bigger districts have more of both (confounding by population size), and more staff find and record more cases (information bias).

points.html: Bradford Hill (1965) listed nine “viewpoints” from which to study an association “before we cry causation”: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. He wrote that none of them “can bring indisputable evidence for or against the cause-and-effect hypothesis and none can be required as a sine qua non”. Temporality is the one that follows from logic: a cause must come before its effect. §17.2.3 treats these viewpoints in full.
Hill also noted that significance tests “remind us of the effects that the play of chance can create” but “contribute nothing to the ‘proof’ of our hypothesis” (Hill, 1965).
A randomised trial answers the confounding question by design: randomisation makes the groups alike, on average, in measured and unmeasured characteristics (§15.9, randomised trials, develops this).
The same caution applies to every measure of association in this book: chi-square tests, risk and odds ratios, and the regression coefficients of Chapters 12–14.
